title: Correlations with Magnetic Activity in the Solar Near-Surface Shear Layer. I. Rotation
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: We used data from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager to determine the rotation rate of the near-surface shear layer and its time variation. We applied the ring-diagram analysis technique allowing us to probe the layer between the depths of 1 Mm and 17 Mm. We find that the rotation rate increases inwards; it reaches values consistent with those inferred from global helioseismic analyses in the deeper layers, however, there are differences in the rotation rate of the northern and southern hemispheres. We show that the time variation of the rotation rate can be determined even without subtracting the time-averaged rotation rate from each epoch; however, such a subtraction is needed to get the canonical ``torsional oscillation'' signal. We find that even at depths as shallow as 1 Mm, the rotation rate shows the typical torsional oscillation pattern. The cumulative zonal displacement inferred from the residual flows exhibits a pronounced high-latitude hemispheric asymmetry and varies on solar-cycle timescales; at $75^\circ$ it shows an apparent temporal association with the polar magnetic field. We find significant correlations between the cumulative displacement and magnetic activity at a subset of latitudes, with multi-year lags: the displacement leads activity by ~5 years near $15^\circ$, whereas at higher latitudes activity leads by ~4 years. At mid to high latitudes, the inferred lags show a hemispheric dependence, with activity tending to lead in the north and lag in the south, suggesting possible hemispheric differences in the timing of cycle evolution and motivating longer time series to test cycle-to-cycle variation.

AI.tldr: This paper uses ring-diagram analysis on Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) data to measure the rotation rate of the near-surface shear layer (1-17 Mm depth) and its time variation. The rotation rate increases inward, shows hemispheric differences, and exhibits the canonical torsional oscillation pattern even at 1 Mm depth. The cumulative zonal displacement shows high-latitude hemispheric asymmetry, correlates with magnetic activity with multi-year lags (displacement leads by ~5 years near 15°, activity leads by ~4 years at higher latitudes), and shows hemispheric-dependent lag patterns suggesting possible differences in cycle timing between hemispheres.
AI.motivation: To determine the rotation rate of the near-surface shear layer and its time variation using HMI data, probing depths of 1-17 Mm with ring-diagram analysis, and to investigate torsional oscillations, cumulative zonal displacement, and their relationship to magnetic activity and solar cycle evolution.
AI.method: Ring-diagram analysis technique applied to Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) data to probe the near-surface shear layer between 1 Mm and 17 Mm depth. Time variation of rotation rate was examined with and without subtracting the time-averaged rotation rate, and cumulative zonal displacement was computed from residual flows and correlated with magnetic activity.
AI.result: Rotation rate increases inward and is consistent with global helioseismic results in deeper layers, yet shows hemispheric differences. Torsional oscillation patterns are present even at 1 Mm depth. Cumulative zonal displacement shows pronounced high-latitude hemispheric asymmetry varying on solar-cycle timescales, with an apparent association with polar magnetic field at 75°. Significant correlations with magnetic activity show multi-year lags: displacement leads activity by ~5 years near 15°, activity leads by ~4 years at higher latitudes. Mid-to-high latitude lags are hemisphere-dependent (activity leads in north, lags in south).
AI.conclusion: The near-surface shear layer rotation can be reliably determined from HMI ring-diagram analysis, revealing torsional oscillations persist to very shallow depths. The cumulative displacement-magnetic activity relationships reveal multi-year lags with hemispheric asymmetries, suggesting possible hemispheric differences in cycle timing and motivating longer time series to assess cycle-to-cycle variations.

title: Low Ly$α$ Visibility in Galaxy Overdensities: Reionization Topology and Neutral-Fraction Ceilings from DIVER over $4.8<z<11$
comment: 30 pages, 17 figures, 3 tables; submitted to ApJ
summary: Ly-alpha emission is widely used to trace cosmic reionization, but its interpretation depends on how Ly-alpha visibility varies with galaxy environment. We use deep JWST/NIRSpec observations from Deep Insights into UV Spectroscopy at the Epoch of Reionization (DIVER) in GOODS-N to measure Ly-alpha visibility for 250 galaxies at 4.8<z<11. The sample contains 84 Ly-alpha detections, including 44 strong emitters with rest-frame Ly-alpha equivalent width W_Lyalpha>25 A. We combine these measurements with H-alpha and [O III] emitters from JWST/NIRCam wide-field slitless spectroscopy to map the density field around each DIVER galaxy. Galaxies with high Ly-alpha equivalent widths (W_Lyalpha>25 A) or high effective Ly-alpha escape fractions (f_esc,Lyalpha^eff>0.05) tend to lie farther from nearby H-alpha and [O III] emitters than galaxies with lower Ly-alpha visibility. The clearest signal occurs near the prominent GOODS-N overdensity at z~5.2, where fewer than 15% of galaxies show strong Ly-alpha emission. This trend is opposite to the simplest inside-out reionization expectation that overdensities produce larger ionized regions and enhance Ly-alpha visibility. Possible explanations include circumgalactic and local intergalactic opacity, dense absorbers, and gas kinematics. We also derive an empirical upper envelope for f_esc,Lyalpha^eff and calibrate it with reionization simulations. Interpreting this envelope as a limiting IGM-attenuation signal gives neutral-fraction ceilings of <x_HI>_max=0.36, 0.76, 0.74, 0.84, and 1.0 at z~5.2, 5.8, 6.7, 7.7, and 9.8, respectively. The z~8 ceiling disfavors an almost completely neutral IGM at this epoch. These results support patchy reionization already underway by z~8 and show that galaxy Ly-alpha visibility encodes both large-scale ionization topology and near-source gas structure.

AI.tldr: This paper uses deep JWST/NIRSpec observations from the DIVER program in GOODS-N to measure Ly-alpha visibility for 250 galaxies at 4.8<z<11, finding that galaxies with strong Ly-alpha emission tend to lie farther from nearby H-alpha/[O III] emitters, opposite to the simplest inside-out reionization expectation. The authors derive an empirical upper envelope for effective Ly-alpha escape fraction, calibrate it with simulations to place neutral-fraction ceilings at various redshifts, and conclude that patchy reionization was already underway by z~8.
AI.motivation: Ly-alpha emission is a critical tracer of cosmic reionization, but its interpretation depends on how Ly-alpha visibility varies with the galaxy environment. Understanding this environmental dependence is essential for correctly interpreting reionization constraints from Ly-alpha observations.
AI.method: Using deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy (DIVER program) in GOODS-N, the authors measure Ly-alpha visibility for 250 galaxies at 4.8<z<11, identifying 84 Ly-alpha detections (44 strong emitters with rest-frame W_Lyalpha>25 A). They combine these with H-alpha and [O III] emitters from JWST/NIRCam slitless spectroscopy to map the density field. They derive an empirical upper envelope for effective Ly-alpha escape fraction and calibrate it with reionization simulations to infer neutral-fraction ceilings.
AI.result: Galaxies with high Ly-alpha equivalent widths or high effective escape fractions tend to lie farther from nearby H-alpha and [O III] emitters. The clearest signal is near the GOODS-N overdensity at z~5.2, where fewer than 15% of galaxies show strong Ly-alpha emission. The empirical envelope gives neutral-fraction ceilings of <x_HI>_max=0.36, 0.76, 0.74, 0.84, and 1.0 at z~5.2, 5.8, 6.7, 7.7, and 9.8, with the z~8 ceiling disfavoring an almost completely neutral IGM at that epoch.
AI.conclusion: The results support patchy reionization already underway by z~8 and show that galaxy Ly-alpha visibility encodes both large-scale ionization topology and near-source gas structure. The observed environmental trend is opposite to the simplest inside-out reionization expectation, suggesting that circumgalactic and local intergalactic opacity, dense absorbers, and gas kinematics play important roles.

title: Correlations with Magnetic Activity in the Solar Near-Surface Shear Layer. II. Radial Shear
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Using Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager ring-diagram measurements and building on the rotation-rate $Ω$ inferences presented in Paper I for depths of 1-17 Mm, we examine the properties of the dimensionless radial shear $\partial\lnΩ/\partial\ln r$. In the radial range overlapping global-mode analyses, the inferred shear agrees with previous results. The near-surface shear layer exhibits a three-region shear structure with an enhanced-shear middle layer, and the largest residual variations occur in the two shallowest regions not accessible to global-mode analyses. We parameterize the enhanced-shear layer by the depth of maximum shear, its amplitude, and its width, and find all three to be strongly correlated with a magnetic activity index; increasing activity corresponds to a shallower, stronger, and modestly narrower layer, indicating that the flows and magnetic fields are interconnected in these layers. This behavior is consistent with expectations that sufficiently strong toroidal fields can enhance the near-surface rotational shear and with inferences of a near-surface toroidal-field concentration near the radius where we observe the strongest shear. Moreover, the observed strengthening and upward shift of the strong-shear layer toward solar-cycle maximum suggest a corresponding solar-cycle dependence in the location of the strong toroidal field. We also highlight the importance of finite-resolution effects and instrumental calibration in interpreting small variations in the results.

AI.tldr: This paper examines the dimensionless radial shear ∂lnΩ/∂lnr in the near-surface shear layer of the Sun using HMI ring-diagram measurements, finding a three-region shear structure with an enhanced-shear middle layer whose depth, amplitude, and width correlate with magnetic activity—stronger activity produces a shallower, stronger, and narrower shear layer, implying coupling between near-surface flows and magnetic fields with solar-cycle dependence.
AI.motivation: To characterize the near-surface shear layer in detail using high-resolution ring-diagram measurements and to understand how rotational shear couples with magnetic activity, particularly in shallow layers not accessible to global-mode analyses.
AI.method: Using Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager ring-diagram measurements, the authors extend Paper I's rotation-rate inferences (depths 1–17 Mm) to analyze the dimensionless radial shear. They parameterize the enhanced-shear layer by three quantities (depth of maximum shear, amplitude, width) and correlate these with a magnetic activity index, while also considering finite-resolution and instrumental calibration effects.
AI.result: Shear values agree with global-mode analyses where ranges overlap. The near-surface shear layer shows a three-region structure with an enhanced middle layer, and the largest residual variations occur in the two shallowest regions. All three shear-layer parameters correlate strongly with magnetic activity: increased activity yields a shallower, stronger, and modestly narrower layer. The strengthening and upward shift of the strong-shear layer toward solar maximum suggests the strong toroidal field also moves upward.
AI.conclusion: The flows and magnetic fields are interconnected in these shallow layers, consistent with the hypothesis that sufficiently strong toroidal fields enhance near-surface rotational shear. A near-surface toroidal-field concentration may exist near the radius of strongest shear, with its location varying over the solar cycle. Finite-resolution effects and instrumental calibration must be considered when interpreting small variations.

title: Detectable subhalo impacts in Milky Way streams
summary: Dark matter subhalos leave gravitational imprints in the stellar streams of the Milky Way. Observing individual strong impacts of subhalos offers a compelling way to constrain and discover potentially dark subhalos down to $10^6 M_\odot$, allowing for new tests of the particle physics properties of dark matter. We develop a pipeline and statistical framework to forecast the expected number of detectable subhalo impacts on stellar streams, based on morphological and kinematic data from surveys such as LSST and Via. Starting from a catalog of confirmed stellar streams, we focus our efforts on 14 promising streams that are relatively well-modeled with a particle spray algorithm. Our criteria for a detectable impact is a deviation at 95% CL from the best-fit polynomial proxy model for the stream, which accounts for stream modeling uncertainties and regulates the effect of distant impacts that are degenerate with these uncertainties. Among the 14 streams studied, we find that 5 streams have an expected number of detectable impacts greater than 0.2. With LSST and Via data, the stream Jet has $5.15^{+1.10}_{-0.95}$ expected detectable impacts, followed by Orphan-Chenab ($1.40^{+0.62}_{-0.47}$), ATLAS-Aliqa Uma ($1.25^{+0.60}_{-0.44}$), GD-1 ($0.55^{+0.43}_{-0.28}$), and Palomar 5 ($0.40^{+0.39}_{-0.23}$), where error bars are the 95% containment on the Poisson mean. These values rely on the assumed subhalo population, which can give a factor of few systematic uncertainty in the predictions. We also consider effects of different particle dark matter models on the number of impacts, finding a suppression by a factor of $\sim 4$ for warm dark matter and fuzzy dark matter models at their current mass bounds and an $O(1)$ enhancement for a toy model of self-interacting dark matter.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a pipeline and statistical framework to forecast detectable dark matter subhalo impacts on 14 well-modeled Milky Way stellar streams using LSST and Via data. They find 5 streams with expected detectable impacts >0.2, with Jet having the highest (5.15), followed by Orphan-Chenab (1.40), ATLAS-Aliqa Uma (1.25), GD-1 (0.55), and Palomar 5 (0.40). The predictions depend on the assumed subhalo population, with warm and fuzzy dark matter models suppressing impacts by ~4x and self-interacting dark matter enhancing them by O(1).
AI.motivation: Dark matter subhalos leave gravitational imprints on stellar streams, and detecting individual impacts from subhalos provides a way to constrain and discover dark subhalos down to 10^6 M_sun, enabling new tests of the particle physics properties of dark matter.
AI.method: The authors develop a pipeline and statistical framework to forecast detectable subhalo impacts on stellar streams. They select 14 well-modeled streams from a confirmed catalog, model them with a particle spray algorithm, and define detection as a deviation at 95% CL from a best-fit polynomial proxy model that accounts for stream modeling uncertainties. They also forecast how different dark matter models (warm, fuzzy, self-interacting) affect the expected count of impacts.
AI.result: Among 14 streams, 5 show expected detectable impacts >0.2: Jet (5.15+1.10/-0.95), Orphan-Chenab (1.40+0.62/-0.47), ATLAS-Aliqa Uma (1.25+0.60/-0.44), GD-1 (0.55+0.43/-0.28), and Palomar 5 (0.40+0.39/-0.23), with 95% containment on the Poisson mean. Warm dark matter and fuzzy dark matter models at current mass bounds suppress impacts by ~4x, while self-interacting dark matter gives O(1) enhancement. Systematic uncertainty from assumed subhalo population can be a factor of few.
AI.conclusion: The forecast demonstrates that upcoming surveys like LSST and Via can enable detection of multiple dark subhalo impacts on stellar streams (particularly Jet), providing a promising avenue for constraining dark matter particle physics properties. The sensitivity depends strongly on the assumed subhalo population and dark matter model, with CDM being most favorable for detection.

title: A Systematic Gaia--ZTF Search for Short-Period Blue Compact-Binary Candidates
summary: We present a catalog of 147 short-period (10.34--106.46~min) blue compact-binary candidates, identified by combining Gaia DR3 astrometry and photometry with ZTF DR23 light curves via a Gaia selection, period searches, and machine-learning morphology ranking. Of these, 111 lack prior compact-binary classifications. Multiwavelength data (DESI DR1, GALEX, AllWISE) reveal a heterogeneous sample: on the Gaia colour--magnitude diagram, 52 sources lie on the white-dwarf locus, 69 in the hot-subdwarf region, and 26 are intermediate. Among 26 sources with DESI spectra, only about one third follow the white-dwarf cooling sequence; the rest are more luminous blue stars with white-dwarf-like low-resolution spectra. We highlight a prioritized subset of new white-dwarf-locus candidates for follow-up, including ten with periods below 40~min and none with existing radial-velocity data. Under fiducial binary assumptions, 17 of these newly identified white-dwarf-locus candidates would exceed the adopted LISA signal-to-noise threshold (led by a 37~pc white dwarf), with the count depending on chirp mass (9 for $0.15\,M_\odot$, 17 for $0.3\,M_\odot$, 21 for $0.6\,M_\odot$), assuming orbital modulation. However, for most of the white-dwarf-locus sample, observed modulation amplitudes exceed any plausible ellipsoidal signal by three to five orders of magnitude, implying that rotating magnetic or chemically inhomogeneous single white dwarfs offer a viable alternative that ZTF photometry alone cannot rule out---the catalog includes at least one confirmed case. We release the full 147-source catalog, including periods, Gaia/spectroscopic classifications, harmonic/ellipsoidal diagnostics, and supplementary tables of fiducial GW estimates and UV--IR photometry.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a catalog of 147 short-period blue compact-binary candidates identified by combining Gaia DR3 astrometry/photometry with ZTF DR23 light curves. Of these, 111 are new classifications. Multiwavelength data reveal a heterogeneous sample across white-dwarf and hot-subdwarf loci. A prioritized subset of ~17 white-dwarf-locus candidates could be detectable by LISA, though large modulation amplitudes suggest rotating magnetic or chemically inhomogeneous single white dwarfs as viable alternatives that ZTF photometry alone cannot rule out.
AI.motivation: To systematically identify and characterize short-period compact-binary candidates—potential LISA gravitational-wave sources—using large-scale astrometric, photometric, and time-domain survey data, while distinguishing genuine binaries from single rotating white dwarfs.
AI.method: Combined Gaia DR3 astrometry and photometry with ZTF DR23 light curves, applying a Gaia selection, period searching, and machine-learning morphology ranking. Followed by multiwavelength characterization using DESI DR1 spectra, GALEX UV, and AllWISE IR photometry, plus fiducial LISA detectability estimates assuming binary parameters.
AI.result: Identified 147 candidates (periods 10.34–106.46 min), with 111 lacking prior classifications. Sources distribute across white-dwarf (52), hot-subdwarf (69), and intermediate (26) loci. Of 26 DESI spectra, ~1/3 follow the WD cooling sequence. 17 white-dwarf-locus candidates exceed the LISA SNR threshold (count varies with chirp mass: 9–21). However, observed modulation amplitudes exceed plausible ellipsoidal signals by 3–5 orders of magnitude for most WD-locus sources, suggesting rotating single WDs as an alternative; at least one confirmed case exists.
AI.conclusion: The catalog provides a valuable resource for compact-binary follow-up and LISA source targeting, but ZTF photometry alone cannot distinguish genuine binaries from rotating magnetic or chemically inhomogeneous single white dwarfs. Full 147-source catalog is released with periods, classifications, diagnostics, and supplementary tables.

title: Serendipitous discovery of an almost-dark galaxy in the Virgo Cluster
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A Letters
summary: Analogues of extreme Local Group galaxies with very low surface brightness and large effective radii must exist elsewhere, still hidden due to current detection limits. We report the serendipitous discovery of a low-mass almost-dark galaxy TTT J1237327+143535 in the Virgo Cluster, observed using the Two-meter Twin Telescope at the Teide Observatory. TTT J1237327+143535 has a central surface brightness of $27.9 \pm 0.2 \, \mathrm{mag arcsec}^{-2}$ in the $g'$-band, an effective radius of $0.9 \pm 0.1 \, \mathrm{kpc}$, and a total stellar mass of $(2.2 \pm 0.4) \times 10^6 \, \mathrm{M_\odot}$. Its effective radius and absolute magnitude are similar to those of galaxies And XXI and And XXIII. The discovery of this extremely low surface brightness, extended, low-mass galaxy suggests the existence of a significant population of almost-dark galaxies in the Virgo Cluster. An in-depth analysis of the Next Generation Virgo Cluster survey, as well as upcoming Rubin Data Releases and the 10-year Rubin Legacy Survey of Space and Time are expected to reveal large samples of this extreme galaxy population, which offers insights on galaxy formation in extreme conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the serendipitous discovery of TTT J1237327+143535, an extremely low surface brightness, low-mass "almost-dark" galaxy in the Virgo Cluster with a central surface brightness of 27.9 mag arcsec⁻², effective radius of 0.9 kpc, and stellar mass of ~2.2×10⁶ M☉, resembling Local Group galaxies And XXI and And XXIII. The discovery suggests a significant hidden population of such extreme galaxies, with future surveys (NGVS reruns, Rubin LSST) expected to uncover large samples.
AI.motivation: To uncover and characterize the hidden population of extremely low surface brightness, extended, low-mass galaxies that are analogues of extreme Local Group galaxies, which remain undetected due to current observational limits.
AI.method: Serendipitous detection using the Two-meter Twin Telescope at the Teide Observatory, followed by photometric and structural analysis (surface brightness, effective radius, stellar mass measurements).
AI.result: Discovery of TTT J1237327+143535 in the Virgo Cluster: central surface brightness of 27.9±0.2 mag arcsec⁻² (g'-band), effective radius of 0.9±0.1 kpc, stellar mass of (2.2±0.4)×10⁶ M☉, with properties similar to And XXI and And XXIII.
AI.conclusion: The existence of this almost-dark galaxy implies a significant population of such extreme objects in the Virgo Cluster; future deep surveys (Next Generation Virgo Cluster survey analysis, Rubin Data Releases and 10-year LSST) are expected to reveal large samples, providing insights into galaxy formation under extreme conditions.

title: Non-ideal MHD and protostellar feedback effects on disc formation and evolution in numerical simulations of star cluster formation
comment: 35 pages, 39 figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS. Published version available at https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stag1501
summary: While recent surveys have resolved hundreds of nearby protostellar discs, numerical simulations assuming ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) have historically struggled to achieve disc formation due to efficient angular momentum removal by magnetic torques. Non-ideal MHD effects, relevant at the low ionization fractions typical of molecular clouds, have been shown to reduce the effectiveness of magnetic braking and promote disc formation. In this work, we present the results from a suite of calculations following the gravitational collapse of 50 $M_{\odot}$ turbulent molecular cloud cores down to the formation and evolution of stellar systems and protostellar discs. We use the radiation-MHD code GIZMO including non-ideal MHD (Ohmic resistivity, ambipolar diffusion, and the Hall effect) and the STARFORGE numerical framework for modeling star formation and stellar feedback. We compare the effects of assuming ideal vs. non-ideal MHD and including sub-grid protostellar jet feedback on disc formation and evolution. Discs form in all of our models but are least massive in the model with ideal MHD and sub-grid jet feedback. Apart from the ideal MHD$+$jets model, we do not observe any significant differences in disc properties between the ideal and non-ideal MHD models; however, ideal MHD discs are embedded in smaller rotating envelopes. Disc sizes are in general agreement with those of observed discs. Jet feedback increases core fragmentation and reduces final stellar masses. Our results suggest that magnetic braking does not efficiently suppress disc formation, regardless of whether ideal or non-ideal MHD is assumed, under the dynamical conditions in which multiple stellar systems form.

AI.tldr: This work presents radiation-MHD simulations of gravitational collapse of 50 M☉ turbulent cores using GIZMO with non-ideal MHD and STARFORGE, finding that discs form in all models regardless of ideal vs non-ideal MHD assumptions, with jet feedback being the main differentiator in disc mass.
AI.motivation: Recent surveys have resolved hundreds of protostellar discs, yet ideal MHD simulations historically struggle to form discs due to efficient magnetic braking removing angular momentum. Non-ideal MHD effects may reduce magnetic braking, but the relative importance of these effects and sub-grid jet feedback on disc formation remains unclear and warrants systematic comparison.
AI.method: The authors run a suite of calculations following gravitational collapse of 50 M☉ turbulent molecular cloud cores using the radiation-MHD code GIZMO, incorporating non-ideal MHD (Ohmic resistivity, ambipolar diffusion, Hall effect) and the STARFORGE framework for star formation and feedback. They compare ideal vs non-ideal MHD models with and without sub-grid protostellar jet feedback.
AI.result: Discs form in all models but are least massive in the ideal MHD+jets case. Apart from that model, disc properties show no significant differences between ideal and non-ideal MHD; however, ideal MHD discs are embedded in smaller rotating envelopes. Disc sizes agree with observed discs. Jet feedback increases core fragmentation and reduces final stellar masses.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic braking does not efficiently suppress disc formation regardless of ideal or non-ideal MHD assumptions under dynamical conditions where multiple stellar systems form. Jet feedback, rather than the MHD treatment, is the major factor controlling disc masses.

title: Reconstructing orbits of galaxies in extreme regions (roger v2.0): an extension to intermediate mass systems
comment: Code hosted at https://github.com/Martindelosrios/pyROGER. Prepared for submission to MNRAS
summary: In this paper, we present an updated version of the roger code, called roger v2.0, developed to perform the orbital classification of galaxies residing in and around galaxy groups and clusters. In addition to the projected phase-space coordinates, the new version incorporates the host halo mass as an additional input parameter. Although the inclusion of the halo mass leads to only modest changes in the classification, it contributes to improving the overall robustness of the method. We also extend the range of host halo masses over which roger can be applied, enabling the analysis of systems with masses down to $10^{13.5} h^{-1} M_{\odot}$. We further provide a Python implementation of the new code, which will be made publicly available. This implementation enables users to efficiently and robustly classify arbitrary galaxy samples using either version of the method. Moreover, it allows users to train a customized classifier on an alternative training set, providing the flexibility to adapt the method to different datasets and scientific applications.

AI.tldr: This paper presents roger v2.0, an updated version of the roger code for orbital classification of galaxies in and around galaxy groups and clusters. The new version incorporates host halo mass as an additional input parameter, extends the applicable halo mass range down to 10^13.5 h^-1 M_sun, and provides a public Python implementation that also allows users to train customized classifiers.
AI.motivation: To improve the roger code for orbital classification of galaxies by incorporating host halo mass as an additional input parameter, extending its applicability to lower mass systems, and providing a flexible, publicly available Python implementation for broader use.
AI.method: The updated roger v2.0 adds host halo mass as an input parameter to the projected phase-space coordinates for orbital classification. It extends the host halo mass range to systems down to 10^13.5 h^-1 M_sun and provides a Python implementation that supports both classification of arbitrary galaxy samples and training of customized classifiers on alternative training sets.
AI.result: The inclusion of halo mass leads to modest changes in classification outcomes but improves the overall robustness of the method. The code is now applicable to a wider range of host halo masses and is made publicly available as a Python implementation.
AI.conclusion: roger v2.0 represents an enhanced, more robust and flexible tool for orbital classification of galaxies in groups and clusters, with broader applicability and public availability for the scientific community.

title: The Kick Velocities of Neutron Stars in Binary Systems
comment: 38 pages, 23 figures, to be submitted to ApJ
summary: Neutron stars (NSs) receive natal kicks on their formation in supernovae (SNe). We consider constraints placed on the natal kick magnitudes by NSs in different kinds of binary systems. We compare observed systems to predictions from the COMPAS rapid population synthesis code, where we apply kick models with varied natal kick prescriptions. Specifically, we compare binary orbits (i.e., periods and eccentricities) and systemic kick estimates of (1) Gaia observations of NS-harboring binaries (Gaia NSs), (2) NS low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs), (3) NS-white dwarf binaries (NSWDs), (4) NS high-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs) and in particular Be X-ray binaries (BeXBs), and (5) double NSs (DNSs). In this comparison, we find that we can reproduce most of the observed properties of the Gaia NSs, LMXBs, and NSWDs with natal kicks calibrated to the velocities of young isolated pulsars, although we need "rocket" kicks to explain the Gaia NS eccentricities. The HMXBs and DNSs, in contrast, show evidence of significantly reduced NS natal kicks. In particular, we find that an apparent correlation between eccentricity and systemic kick for DNSs can be explained by Blaauw kicks, if the natal kicks are ${\lesssim}\,10\,$km$\,$s$^{-1}$. Although our model does not align well with low-metallicity Gaia NSs, high-eccentricity BeXBs, and DNS mass estimates, we provide alternative hypothetical explanations for these systems. We conclude that a model in which NSs that are formed in binaries with high-mass companions receive significantly reduced natal kicks can provide a relatively consistent explanation for the observed NSs in binary systems.

AI.tldr: This paper compares observed neutron star (NS) binary systems across five categories—Gaia NSs, LMXBs, NSWDs, HMXBs/BeXBs, and DNSs—against COMPAS rapid population synthesis predictions using varied natal kick prescriptions. The authors find that most observed properties of Gaia NSs, LMXBs, and NSWDs can be reproduced with kicks calibrated to isolated pulsar velocities, but HMXBs and DNSs require significantly reduced natal kicks (≲10 km/s for DNSs, where eccentricity–systemic kick correlations are explained by Blaauw kicks). They conclude that NSs formed in binaries with high-mass companions receive substantially reduced natal kicks.
AI.motivation: To place empirical constraints on neutron star natal kick magnitudes by leveraging a wide variety of observed NS-bearing binary systems, testing whether a single kick prescription can reconcile observations or whether formation environment (binary, companion mass) must influence kick strength.
AI.method: The authors compare observed binary orbital properties (periods, eccentricities) and systemic kick estimates from five classes of NS binaries against predictions from the COMPAS rapid population synthesis code, which employs different natal kick models. They identify consistent and inconsistent features across system types and use discrepancies (e.g., DNS eccentricity–kick correlation) to constrain kick parameters.
AI.result: Standard pulsar-calibrated kicks reproduce Gaia NSs, LMXBs, and NSWDs (though "rocket" kicks are needed for Gaia NS eccentricities). HMXBs and DNSs require greatly reduced natal kicks. DNS eccentricity–systemic kick correlation is explained by Blaauw kicks with natal kicks ≲10 km/s. Some mismatches remain (low-metallicity Gaia NSs, high-eccentricity BeXBs, DNS mass estimates), for which alternative explanations are proposed.
AI.conclusion: A model where NSs formed in binaries with high-mass companions receive significantly reduced natal kicks consistently explains observed NSs across binary systems, though some subpopulations require additional or alternative mechanisms.

title: Tracing Lyman alpha escape in the CRISTAL-02 galaxy at z~5.3
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, 1 table. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary:
Aim. We investigate the mechanisms regulating Lyman-alpha (Ly-a) escape in the star-forming galaxy CRISTAL-02 at z~5.3. The galaxy hosts five distinct clumps, with Clumps A and B suggested as potential active galactic nuclei (AGN) candidates. We study how AGN or star formation activity influences the spatial distribution and escape of Ly-a emission.
  Methods. Using VLT/MUSE Ly-a and JWST/NIRSpec IFU H-a and H-b observations, complemented by NIRCam UV imaging, we constructed spatially matched emission-line maps. We derived flux, line-ratio, and extinction maps, together with spatially resolved Ly-a escape fractions and ionizing photon production efficiencies.
  Results. Ly-a emission extends preferentially along the [C ii] outflow direction, while H-a and UV trace the galactic disk. Clumps A and B show contrasting properties: Clump A, with lower dust attenuation, exhibits enhanced Ly-a/H-a ratios and a higher Ly-a escape fraction, whereas Clump B shows stronger H-a and UV emission but suppressed Ly-a. These results suggest that Ly-a escape is influenced by outflows, dust attenuation, and local gas conditions.
  Conclusions. We present spatially resolved measurements of the Ly-a escape fraction and ionizing photon production efficiency in a galaxy at z~5.3, highlighting the role of feedback-driven gas clearing and anisotropic outflows in shaping Ly-a emission. The evidence favors an outflow, but the available data cannot uniquely distinguish between AGN- and star formation-driven feedback. Future spatially resolved Ly-a, H-a, and [C ii] observations will be crucial for identifying the dominant feedback mechanism.

AI.tldr: This study investigates Lyα escape mechanisms in the star-forming galaxy CRISTAL-02 at z~5.3 using VLT/MUSE and JWST/NIRSpec IFU observations. The authors find that Lyα emission preferentially extends along the [C ii] outflow direction, while Clump A shows higher Lyα escape fraction due to lower dust attenuation, whereas Clump B exhibits suppressed Lyα despite stronger Hα and UV emission. Evidence favors outflow-driven gas clearing, but the data cannot uniquely distinguish between AGN- and star-formation-driven feedback.
AI.motivation: To understand what regulates Lyman-alpha escape in high-redshift galaxies, and to determine whether AGN or star formation activity influences the spatial distribution and escape of Lyα emission in a galaxy with multiple clumps, some of which are potential AGN candidates.
AI.method: Using spatially matched emission-line maps built from VLT/MUSE Lyα, JWST/NIRSpec IFU Hα and Hβ observations, and NIRCam UV imaging, the authors derive flux, line-ratio, and extinction maps, along with spatially resolved Lyα escape fractions and ionizing photon production efficiencies.

title: SN 2021pfs: A Type Ia Supernova Likely Affected by Progenitor Metallicity, as Revealed by Comparison with Its Twin Counterpart
comment: 35 pages, 14 figures, published in SCIENCE CHINA Physics, Mechanics & Astronomy,DOI: 10.1007/s11433-026-2999-3
summary: We present extensive photometric and spectroscopic observations of the normal type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) 2021pfs, which occurred in the Seyfert 2 galaxy NGC 5427 at a redshift 0.009. title: The VariableTNG project: mass-dependent regulation of galaxy morphology by baryonic feedback
summary: Galaxy morphology is shaped by both assembly history and baryonic processes, but their relative roles remain uncertain. We use the VariableTNG (VTNG) simulation suite to investigate how variations in baryonic feedback regulate galaxy morphology while keeping the initial conditions fixed. VTNG consists of cosmological magnetohydrodynamic simulations performed with the moving-mesh code {\sc AREPO}, varying eight parameters governing stellar and AGN feedback. At $z=1$, we characterize morphology using $κ_{\rm co}$, $v/σ$, and the axis ratio $c/a$. We find substantial morphological diversity across feedback models, with the dominant mechanism strongly dependent on stellar mass. For $M_\ast \lesssim 10^{11}\,{\rm M_\odot}$, morphology is primarily controlled by the supernova temperature $T_{\rm SN}$: larger $T_{\rm SN}$ delays early star formation, promotes a denser and more rotationally supported gas reservoir, and favours subsequent disc growth through in-situ star formation. At higher masses, morphology becomes increasingly sensitive to AGN feedback, particularly the quasar-mode coupling efficiency $ε_{\rm f,high}$. Higher $ε_{\rm f,high}$ suppresses early black hole growth, thereby weakening subsequent radio-mode feedback associated with gas depletion and loss of rotational support. The resulting morphology--mass relation is non-monotonic, with maximum rotational support at intermediate stellar masses. Our results demonstrate that baryonic feedback regulates galaxy morphology through distinct mass-dependent pathways, with stellar feedback dominating at lower masses and AGN self-regulation becoming increasingly important at the massive end.

The authors find that stellar feedback (specifically supernova temperature) dominates morphology at lower masses, while AGN feedback (quasar-mode coupling efficiency) becomes increasingly important at higher masses, resulting in a non-monotonic morphology-mass relation with maximum rotational support at intermediate masses.
AI.motivation: The relative roles of assembly history and baryonic processes in shaping galaxy morphology remain uncertain. The authors aim to disentangle these contributions by systematically varying baryonic feedback parameters in cosmological simulations while holding initial conditions fixed.
AI.method: The study uses the VariableTNG (VTNG) simulation suite, which consists of cosmological magnetohydrodynamic simulations run with the moving-mesh code AREPO. Eight parameters governing stellar and AGN feedback are varied while initial conditions are kept fixed. Galaxy morphology is characterized at z=1 using three metrics: κ_co, v/σ, and the axis ratio c/a.

At higher masses, morphology becomes sensitive to the quasar-mode coupling efficiency ε_f,high, where higher values suppress early black hole growth and weaken radio-mode feedback. The resulting morphology-mass relation is non-monotonic, with maximum rotational support at intermediate stellar masses.
AI.conclusion: Baryonic feedback regulates galaxy morphology through distinct mass-dependent pathways: stellar feedback dominates at lower masses, while AGN self-regulation becomes increasingly important at the massive end.

title: Chromospheric heating and magnetic topology above the shared penumbra of a delta-spot: Multi-line inversions and multi-height magnetic-field extrapolations
summary: We analysed observations of the Fe I 617.3 nm, Ca II 854.2 nm, and Ca II H lines obtained with CRISP and CHROMIS at the SST. Spatially coupled non-LTE inversions constrained the chromospheric atmosphere, while the WFA provided estimates of the chromospheric line-of-sight magnetic field. We combined these photospheric and chromospheric constraints with an HMI magnetogram as input to a multi-height field extrapolation. We characterised the reconstructed topology using the twist number, squashing factor, current density, and field-line connectivity. Results. The Ca II H magnetic signal is concentrated mainly above the strongest photospheric field concentrations, whereas Ca II 854.2 nm yields stronger and more spatially extended line-of-sight fields. The chromosphere above the shared penumbra is approximately 300 K hotter than nearby quiet regions. The selected brightening follows a chromospheric loop, with enhanced temperature and a transition from blueshift to redshift along the structure. The extrapolation recovers field strengths broadly consistent with the inversions and reveals a left-handed, flux-rope-like core following the polarity inversion line. Enhanced currents and connectivity gradients occur near parts of its boundary, where field lines connect the twisted structure to overarching loops. Conclusions. The temperature and velocity patterns and magnetic topology are consistent with reconnection between the twisted polarity-inversion-line field and the surrounding loops, depositing energy in the chromosphere and driving plasma along reconfigured field lines. These signatures do not uniquely establish reconnection, but show that combining high-resolution spectropolarimetric inversions with multi-height extrapolations can relate chromospheric energy release to the local three-dimensional magnetic structure.

The authors find a left-handed flux-rope-like structure along the polarity inversion line, enhanced temperatures (~300 K hotter) and velocity gradients along a brightening, and interpret the combined signatures as consistent with reconnection between the twisted field and surrounding loops.
AI.motivation: To understand how chromospheric energy release relates to the local three-dimensional magnetic structure, using high-resolution observations and multi-height extrapolations to connect energy deposition to magnetic topology.

Applied spatially coupled non-LTE inversions to constrain the chromosphere, used the weak-field approximation (WFA) for chromospheric line-of-sight magnetic fields, and combined photospheric HMI magnetogram data with these constraints to perform a multi-height field extrapolation. Characterized topology using twist number, squashing factor, current density, and field-line connectivity.

The chromosphere above the shared penumbra is ~300 K hotter than quiet regions. The brightening follows a chromospheric loop with enhanced temperature and blueshift-to-redshift transition. The extrapolation recovers field strengths consistent with inversions and reveals a left-handed flux-rope-like core along the polarity inversion line, with enhanced currents and connectivity gradients near its boundary.
AI.conclusion: The temperature, velocity, and magnetic topology signatures are consistent with reconnection between the twisted polarity-inversion-line field and surrounding loops, depositing energy in the chromosphere and driving plasma along reconfigured field lines. While not uniquely establishing reconnection, the study demonstrates that combining high-resolution spectropolarimetric inversions with multi-height extrapolations can effectively relate chromospheric energy release to the local 3D magnetic structure.

title: The UKIRT M33 Monitoring Project: A 15-Year Near-Infrared Variable Star Catalogue for the Central Kiloparsec, and Prospects for Star Formation History and Dust Return
comment: To appear in the Proceedings of IAU Symposium 405, Traversing the Galactic Center in Space and Time
summary: We present results from the UKIRT M33 Monitoring Project, a near-infrared survey of variable red giants in the Local Group spiral galaxy M33. Combining four independent photometric datasets spanning UIST (2003), UFTI (2005), WFCAM (2005-2007), and a new UKIRT Hemisphere Survey epoch (2018), we construct a homogenised 15.11-year $K$-band light-curve catalogue for 847 stars in the central kiloparsec, of which 771 (91 per cent) are variable. Cross-matching with archival Spitzer photometry identifies 120 dust-enshrouded AGB candidates. We compare the spatial coverage of this central catalogue with the earlier UIST-only (Paper I) and disc-wide WFCAM (Paper IV) variable-star surveys. Building on this catalogue, two forthcoming papers will (i) measure individual pulsation periods to reconstruct the star formation history of the central kiloparsec, and (ii) refine dust and gas mass-loss rates across the disc using the extended time baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the UKIRT M33 Monitoring Project, a homogenised 15.11-year K-band light-curve catalogue of 847 stars (91% variable) in the central kiloparsec of the Local Group spiral galaxy M33, built from four independent photometric datasets between 2003-2018. Cross-matching with Spitzer identifies 120 dust-enshrouded AGB candidates. Two forthcoming papers will use this catalogue for star formation history reconstruction and dust/gas mass-loss rate refinement.
AI.motivation: To construct a long-baseline, homogenised near-infrared variable-star catalogue for the central region of M33, enabling studies of evolved red giants, AGB stars, and the star formation history of the galaxy.
AI.method: Combining four independent photometric datasets (UIST 2003, UFTI 2005, WFCAM 2005-2007, and a new UKIRT Hemisphere Survey epoch 2018), constructing a homogenised 15.11-year K-band light-curve catalogue for 847 stars in the central kiloparsec, and cross-matching with archival Spitzer photometry.
AI.result: A catalogue of 847 stars, of which 771 (91%) are variable; 120 dust-enshrouded AGB candidates identified via Spitzer cross-matching; spatial coverage comparison made with earlier UIST-only and disc-wide variable-star surveys.
AI.conclusion: The extended time baseline catalogue will enable two forthcoming studies: (i) measuring individual pulsation periods to reconstruct the star formation history of the central kiloparsec, and (ii) refining dust and gas mass-loss rates across the disc.

title: Toward Operational Solar Flare Peak Flux Nowcasting: A Strategy Combining Real-Time Data, Machine Learning, and NOAA Flare Detection Criteria
summary: We present the RMN strategy (Real-time data, machine learning, and NOAA flare detection criteria) for nowcasting the peak soft X-ray flux of ongoing solar flares under operationally realistic conditions. The strategy combines real-time GOES 0.1-0.8 nm X-ray observations with an attention-based sequence-to-sequence Long Short-Term Memory model. Under the NOAA flare detection criteria, predictions are evaluated at one-minute intervals from three minutes after the cataloged onset to the observed peak using the preceding 60 minutes of X-ray observations. We apply the RMN strategy to C-, M-, and X-class flares observed by GOES-8-18 from 1997 to 2024 using four-fold cross-validation. The major results of this study are as follows. First, the model nowcasts peak soft X-ray flux with RMSE and PE values of 0.26 and 3.11\% for the $\geq$C-class group, 0.45 and 5.59\% for the $\geq$M-class group, and 0.87 and 12.76\% for the X-class group. The higher discrepancy toward stronger flare groups indicates that peak-flux prediction is more challenging for higher-intensity flares. Second, the model performance depends on flare rise time and prediction time, with larger errors for longer rise time events and improved performance as the prediction time approaches the flare peak. Shorter rise time events approach their final peak more rapidly, providing a clearer indication of the eventual peak, whereas the larger difference for longer rise time events may partly reflect more complex temporal evolution. Third, empirical coverage based on total uncertainty remains high but decreases for stronger flares, with noise uncertainty contributing more than model uncertainty.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the RMN strategy, which combines real-time GOES X-ray observations with an attention-based sequence-to-sequence LSTM model to nowcast the peak soft X-ray flux of ongoing solar flares under NOAA detection criteria. Evaluated on GOES-8-18 data from 1997-2024, the model achieves RMSE values of 0.26, 0.45, and 0.87 for C-, M-, and X-class flares respectively, with performance depending on flare rise time and prediction time.
AI.motivation: To develop an operationally realistic nowcasting framework for predicting the peak soft X-ray flux of solar flares in real-time, addressing the challenge that peak-flux prediction becomes increasingly difficult for higher-intensity flare classes.
AI.method: The RMN strategy integrates three components: (1) real-time GOES 0.1-0.8 nm X-ray observations, (2) an attention-based sequence-to-sequence Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model, and (3) NOAA flare detection criteria. Predictions are made at one-minute intervals from three minutes after cataloged onset to the observed peak, using the preceding 60 minutes of X-ray data. The model is validated via four-fold cross-validation on C-, M-, and X-class flares from GOES-8-18 (1997-2024).
AI.result: The model achieves RMSE values of 0.26 (PE 3.11%), 0.45 (PE 5.59%), and 0.87 (PE 12.76%) for the ≥C-, ≥M-, and X-class flare groups respectively. Performance improves as prediction time approaches the flare peak, with shorter rise-time flares being easier to predict. Empirical uncertainty coverage remains high but decreases for stronger flares, with noise uncertainty dominating over model uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: The RMN strategy provides an effective operational nowcasting framework for solar flare peak flux prediction, though accuracy degrades for stronger flares and longer rise-time events. The decomposition of total uncertainty reveals that noise-related uncertainty is the dominant contributor, suggesting where future improvements could focus.

title: Diversity of Ionized Gas Structures in Nearby Metal-poor Dwarf Galaxies
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to PASJ. Comments are very welcome!
summary: We investigate whether optical and far-infrared [O III] emission from nearby metal-poor dwarf galaxies can be represented by a homogeneous one-zone ionized-gas model with a single electron temperature and density. Our sample comprises five galaxies from the Herschel Dwarf Galaxy Survey: HS1222+3741, SBS0335-052E, POX186, Haro11, and IZw18. We combine galaxy-integrated or nearly galaxy-integrated [O III] 4363 and 5007 measurements from Seimei/KOOLS-IFU observations and published or archival spectroscopy with Herschel/PACS [O III] 88um measurements. Because [O III] 4363 is not detected in HS1222+3741, the analysis is based on the remaining four galaxies. SBS0335-052E and Haro11 lie near or slightly beyond the low-density boundary of the one-zone diagnostic. Their nominal line ratios favor effective densities of ne<1cm-3, while conservative treatment of the uncertainties allows values up to 40 and 10cm-3, respectively. These remain substantially below densities inferred from independent diagnostics. By contrast, POX186 and IZw18 show no significant discrepancy between the optical--far-infrared [O III] and low-ionization optical diagnostics. Additional optical and ultraviolet diagnostics show that inferred densities can span several orders of magnitude within a galaxy. Representative two-zone models reproduce the [O III] 4363, 5007, and 88um emission in SBS0335-052E and Haro11 by combining relatively dense gas with cooler, low-density gas. The low-density component contributes approximately 61% and 72% of the 88um luminosity, but only 14% and 23% of the 5007 luminosity, respectively. These solutions are not unique and may represent a broader unresolved distribution of gas conditions. Our results show that temperatures and densities inferred from integrated one-zone analyses are effective quantities and that similar diagnostic discrepancies can arise in nearby metal-poor galaxies.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether nearby metal-poor dwarf galaxies can be described by a homogeneous one-zone ionized-gas model with single temperature and density, using combined optical and far-infrared [O III] emission from five galaxies. For SBS0335-052E and Haro11, the one-zone model predicts inconsistent (too low) densities, while POX186 and IZw18 show no such discrepancy. Two-zone models reproduce the observations and reveal that a dominant low-density, cooler component contributes most of the 88um flux but little of the 5007 flux, demonstrating that integrated one-zone analyses yield only effective quantities.
AI.motivation: To determine whether spatially integrated optical and far-infrared [O III] line measurements from metal-poor dwarf galaxies can be self-consistently explained by a simple one-zone photoionization model with a single electron temperature and density, or whether more complex multi-phase structures are required.
AI.method: The authors compare galaxy-integrated [O III] 4363 and 5007 measurements from Seimei/KOOLS-IFU observations and archival spectroscopy with Herschel/PACS [O III] 88um data for five galaxies from the Herschel Dwarf Galaxy Survey. They place these line ratios on one-zone diagnostic diagrams, conservatively propagate uncertainties, compare with independent diagnostics (optical/UV), and explore representative two-zone models to reproduce the emission in discrepant galaxies.
AI.result: SBS0335-052E and Haro11 fall near or beyond the low-density boundary of the one-zone diagnostic, favoring effective densities ne<1 cm^-3, with conservative upper limits up to 40 and 10 cm^-3, respectively—substantially below densities from independent diagnostics. POX186 and IZw18 show no significant discrepancy. Two-zone models reproduce the data: a low-density component contributes ~61% and 72% of the 88um luminosity but only ~14% and 23% of the 5007 luminosity for SBS0335-052E and Haro11, respectively, though solutions are not unique.
AI.conclusion: Temperatures and densities derived from integrated one-zone analyses are effective quantities rather than representative physical values. Similar diagnostic discrepancies can arise in nearby metal-poor galaxies, necessitating multi-zone or spatially resolved modeling to infer the true gas conditions.

title: ALOHA IRDCs Molecular Line Follow-up: I. Gas properties and kinematics
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, accepted for publication on A&A
summary: Infrared Dark Clouds are ideal sites for investigating the initial conditions of massive star and cluster formation. The A Lei Of the Habitat and Assembly of Infrared Dark Clouds (ALOHA IRDCs), a James Clerk Maxwell Telescope (JCMT) Large Program, has mapped nearby IRDCs with SCUBA-2. Complementary molecular line observations are needed to characterise the physical, kinematic, and chemical properties of the dense gas. We aim to determine the thermal, kinematic, and chemical properties of clumps identified in the ALOHA IRDCs, and to assess their evolutionary status and level of star-forming activity. We performed single-pointing K-band and W-band observations towards 56 ALOHA IRDCs clumps using the Effelsberg 100-m and Yebes 40-m telescopes, respectively. We derived NH3 kinetic temperatures using the hyperfine group ratio (HFGR) method and identified infall and shock signatures from HCO+, H13CO+, SiO, and HNCO profiles. Water masers and NH2D emission were used as complementary tracers of chemical evolution and star formation. The clumps exhibit kinetic temperatures of 15-29 K. We detect NH2D emission towards 18 sources, with NH2D centroid velocities consistent with NH3, indicating both species trace the same dense gas component. More than half of the clumps display blue-asymmetric HCO+ profiles, identifying them as infall candidates. Water masers are detected in 22 sources, with prominent velocity ranges and variability. Broad SiO emission (>~20 km/s) indicates strong shocks, while narrower extents (<~6km/s) likely trace large-scale interactions or low-velocity shocks. The widespread infall signatures, shock tracers, masers, and NH2D emission suggest that relatively quiescent, chemically young material can coexist with dynamically active gas affected by early protostellar feedback, providing insight into the coupled physical and chemical evolution of massive IRDC clumps.

Clumps show kinetic temperatures of 15-29 K, widespread infall signatures (blue-asymmetric HCO+ profiles in over half), 22 water masers, broad SiO emission indicating shocks, and NH2D detection toward 18 sources. Results reveal coexistence of quiescent chemically young material with dynamically active gas influenced by early protostellar feedback.

Complementary molecular line observations are needed to characterize the physical, kinematic, and chemical properties of dense gas within IRDC clumps, particularly to assess their evolutionary status and star-forming activity.
AI.method: Single-pointing K-band (Effelsberg 100-m) and W-band (Yebes 40-m) observations of 56 ALOHA IRDC clumps. NH3 kinetic temperatures were derived via the hyperfine group ratio (HFGR) method. Infall and shock signatures were identified from HCO+, H13CO+, SiO, and HNCO profiles. Water masers and NH2D emission served as complementary tracers of chemical evolution and star formation.
AI.result: Clumps have kinetic temperatures of 15-29 K. NH2D detected toward 18 sources with centroid velocities consistent with NH3. Over half of clumps show blue-asymmetric HCO+ profiles (infall candidates). Water masers detected in 22 sources with notable velocity ranges and variability. Broad SiO emission (>20 km/s) indicates strong shocks, while narrower extents (<6 km/s) trace large-scale interactions or low-velocity shocks.
AI.conclusion: Widespread infall signatures, shock tracers, masers, and NH2D emission suggest that relatively quiescent, chemically young material can coexist with dynamically active gas affected by early protostellar feedback, providing insight into the coupled physical and chemical evolution of massive IRDC clumps.

title: OutThere Survey: Addressing $\mathrm{ξ_{ion}}$ and $\mathrm{f_{esc}}$ with a population of average galaxies at z$\sim$2
summary: Constraining the major contributors to the ionisation of the early universe is an ongoing endeavour of high-redshift galaxy research. We measure the ionising photon production efficiency and Lyman Continuum escape fraction for a sample of 230 intermediate redshift ($1.3<z<2.6$) sources observed as a part of the \textit{OutThere survey}; a pure-parallel, wide-area JWST/NIRISS survey with accompanying JWST/NIRCam, NIRISS and HST photometry. The low threshold emission selection criteria for this sample makes for a large and robust control, against which other works may be contrasted, particularly for low-mass galaxies above z$>$5. This control sample allows us to verify the correlations between ionising and spectral/physical properties suggested by previous studies. We find no significant correlations between the ionising photon production efficiency ($\mathrm{ξ_{ion}}$) with the UV slope, $\mathrm{M_{UV}}$, M$_*$ or sSFR. We do find that $\mathrm{ξ_{ion}}$ correlates with [OIII]5007Å\, equivalent width (EW) (Spearman coefficient $ρ$ =0.24; p$< 4\times10^{-4}$) and H$α$ EW ($ρ$ =0.63; p$<< 1\times10^{-6}$) hold even at low EW albeit with more scatter. We also find that our novel approach to determining the ionising photon escape fraction $\mathrm{f_{esc}}$ results in values within theoretical ranges (0-10\%) though vary substantially in comparison to the empirical results (median $\mathrm{f_{esc}} = 0.9\%^{+1.1}_{-0.5}$ including non-detections, median $\mathrm{f_{esc}} = 1.9\%^{+8.9}_{-1.8}$ above a $0.01\%$ threshold). We find that this escape fraction method has consistently significant correlations with the redshift, SFR and M$_{UV}$ and sample-dependent correlations with [OIII]5007Å\,EW,H$α$ EW and stellar mass.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a sample of 230 intermediate-redshift ($1.3<z<2.6$) galaxies from the OutThere survey (JWST/NIRISS + NIRCam/HST photometry) to measure the ionising photon production efficiency (ξion) and Lyman Continuum escape fraction (fesc). They find no significant correlations between ξion and UV slope, M_UV, M*, or sSFR, but find significant correlations with [OIII]5007Å EW and Hα EW. Their novel fesc determination yields values within theoretical ranges (0–10%), with median fesc = 0.9% (including non-detections). The fesc method shows consistent correlations with redshift, SFR, and M_UV, and sample-dependent correlations with emission-line EWs and stellar mass.
AI.motivation: Understanding the major contributors to reionisation of the early universe is a key open question. This work provides a large, robust low-redshift control sample to validate correlations between ionising properties and galaxy physical/spectral properties that other works rely on when interpreting high-redshift (z>5) observations.
AI.method: They analyse 230 intermediate-redshift ($1.3<z<2.6$) galaxies from the OutThere survey, a pure-parallel wide-area JWST/NIRISS survey with supplementary JWST/NIRCam, NIRISS, and HST photometry. Low-threshold emission selection provides a robust control sample. They measure the ionising photon production efficiency (ξion) and employ a novel approach to determine the Lyman Continuum escape fraction (fesc), using Spearman rank correlation tests to probe relationships with galaxy properties.
AI.result: No significant correlations found between ξion and UV slope, M_UV, M*, or sSFR. Significant positive correlations found between ξion and [OIII]5007Å EW (ρ=0.24; p<4×10^-4) and Hα EW (ρ=0.63; p<<1×10^-6), which persist even at low EW with more scatter. The novel fesc method yields values within theoretical ranges (0–10%), with median fesc = 0.9%+1.1-0.5 (including non-detections) and 1.9%+8.9-1.8 above a 0.01% threshold. fesc shows consistently significant correlations with redshift, SFR, and M_UV, and sample-dependent correlations with [OIII]5007Å EW, Hα EW, and stellar mass.
AI.conclusion: The large control sample validates some previously suggested correlations (with emission-line EWs) while casting doubt on others (UV slope, M_UV, M*, sSFR). The findings provide important calibration for interpreting high-redshift studies of galaxy ionising properties during the epoch of reionisation, with fesc values consistent with theoretical expectations.

title: Re-evaluating the resolved mass-metallicity relation with a self-consistent metallicity calibration
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures, accepted by A&A. Comments are welcome
summary: Aims. The mass-metallicity relation (MZR) is essential for understanding the chemical evolution of galaxies. Whether the star formation rate (SFR) plays a role in setting the metallicity has long been debated. Using various metallicity calibrations can result in different conclusions for this fundamental yet unresolved issue. Methods. We apply a self-consistent metallicity calibration based on photoionization models to re-evaluate the resolved and integrated MZR. We utilize the integral field unit data from SDSS-IV/MaNGA, with $\sim 3.5\times10^6$ spaxels and $\sim$ 4550 galaxies. We compare our preferred metallicity calibration with several strong-line calibrations in the literature and direct method metallicity. We analyze the metallicity residual of MZR to evaluate the effects of SFR and apply the partial correlation coefficient to quantify the effects. Results. The metallicity calibration we used shows the best consistency with the direct method. We provide 3 equations for resolved MZR, and verify that local SFR does not show significant correlation with metallicity. Considering the integrated properties, (s)SFR do not present correlation with the metallicity residuals. The results suggest that an equilibrium of inflow and outflow is favored, and the mass-metallicity relation does not have a secondary dependence on SFR.

AI.tldr: This paper re-evaluates the mass-metallicity relation (MZR) using a self-consistent metallicity calibration based on photoionization models, applied to ~3.5 million spaxels and ~4550 galaxies from SDSS-IV/MaNGA. The authors find that their calibration is most consistent with the direct method and show that neither local nor integrated star formation rate (SFR) correlates significantly with metallicity residuals, concluding that the MZR has no secondary dependence on SFR and that an equilibrium of inflow and outflow is favored.
AI.motivation: To resolve the long-standing debate about whether star formation rate plays a role in setting gas-phase metallicity in galaxies, and to address how different metallicity calibrations can lead to conflicting conclusions on this issue.
AI.method: Applied a self-consistent metallicity calibration based on photoionization models to re-evaluate both resolved and integrated MZRs. Used IFU data from SDSS-IV/MaNGA (~3.5 million spaxels, ~4550 galaxies). Compared their calibration with several strong-line calibrations and the direct method. Analyzed metallicity residuals of the MZR and used partial correlation coefficients to quantify SFR effects.
AI.result: The self-consistent calibration showed the best agreement with the direct method. Three equations for the resolved MZR were produced. Neither local SFR nor integrated (s)SFR showed significant correlation with metallicity or metallicity residuals.
AI.conclusion: The findings support an equilibrium between inflow and outflow as the physical mechanism governing the MZR, and conclude that the mass-metallicity relation does not exhibit a secondary dependence on star formation rate.

title: The Nearby Star Formation and Supernova Histories Reconstructed from Young Star Clusters
comment: 27 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to ApJ. Comments are welcome. An interactive 3D version of Figures 2 and 3 is available at https://cswigg.github.io/cam_website/oviz_figures/oviz_supernovae.html
summary: We reconstruct the recent star formation and core-collapse supernova (ccSN) histories of the Solar Neighborhood from the past trajectories of young star clusters. Using a \textit{Gaia}-based cluster sample with newly derived ages, masses, and bulk 3D velocities, we integrate orbits backward in an assumed axisymmetric Galactic potential and combine the trajectories with IMF sampling and stellar lifetimes to infer ccSN times and locations over the past 50 Myr. The result is an all-sky, 3D, time-resolved map of nearby ccSN activity for comparison with high-resolution 3D views of the local interstellar medium. The 0--15 Myr map shows strong enhancements toward Orion, Vela, Sco--Cen, and Cepheus, many within present-day cavities and shells. At earlier times, the dominant enhancements trace the Collinder 135, Messier 6, and Alpha Persei cluster families, showing how the remnants of massive star-forming complexes have shaped the recent local feedback history. We recover a bursty star formation history followed by a delayed, smoother ccSN history. Over the last 40 Myr, the mean star formation and ccSN rates are \(823~M_\odot~\mathrm{Myr}^{-1}\) and \(7.7~\mathrm{Myr}^{-1}\), respectively, corresponding to a Milky Way rate of \(0.55\pm0.03~\mathrm{century}^{-1}\). Present-day OB-star catalogs yield rates ranging from agreement with the cluster reconstruction to several times higher. Because the catalogs overlap weakly and require different corrections, we do not rescale the ccSN map. Our reconstruction provides an empirical framework for connecting the recent history of massive-star feedback to the 3D structure and life cycle of gas in the nearby Milky Way.

AI.tldr: This paper reconstructs the recent star formation and core-collapse supernova (ccSN) history of the Solar Neighborhood over the past 50 Myr by integrating the backward orbits of Gaia-based young star clusters with known ages, masses, and 3D velocities in an assumed Galactic potential. The resulting all-sky, 3D, time-resolved ccSN map shows enhancements toward Orion, Vela, Sco-Cen, and Cepheus in the recent epoch, traces older cluster families (Collinder 135, Messier 6, Alpha Persei) at earlier times, and recovers a bursty star formation history with mean rates of 823 M_sun/Myr and 7.7 ccSN/Myr (equivalent to 0.55±0.03 per century for the Milky Way).
AI.motivation: To establish an empirical framework connecting the recent history of massive-star feedback to the 3D structure and life cycle of gas in the nearby Milky Way, enabling direct comparison with high-resolution 3D views of the local interstellar medium.
AI.method: The authors use a Gaia-based sample of young star clusters with newly derived ages, masses, and bulk 3D velocities. They integrate cluster orbits backward in time under an assumed axisymmetric Galactic potential, then combine the trajectories with initial mass function (IMF) sampling and stellar lifetimes to infer ccSN times and locations over the past 50 Myr, producing a 3D time-resolved map of nearby ccSN activity.
AI.result: The 0-15 Myr map shows strong ccSN enhancements toward Orion, Vela, Sco-Cen, and Cepheus near present-day cavities and shells. Earlier epochs trace the Collinder 135, Messier 6, and Alpha Persei cluster families. The star formation history is bursty while the ccSN history is smoother and delayed. Mean rates over 40 Myr are 823 M_sun/Myr (star formation) and 7.7 ccSN/Myr, corresponding to a Milky Way rate of 0.55±0.03 per century. Present-day OB-star catalogs yield rates ranging from consistent with the cluster reconstruction to several times higher.
AI.conclusion: The reconstruction provides an empirical, all-sky 3D time-resolved framework for connecting recent massive-star feedback to the surrounding ISM structure and gas lifecycle. Since OB-star catalogs overlap weakly with cluster reconstruction and require different corrections, the ccSN map is not rescaled, but the framework offers a template for future comparisons.

title: An Optical Illusion: High Electron Densities Create Extremely Metal-Poor Galaxy Impostors
summary: JWST has enabled the discovery of dozens of extremely metal-poor galaxies (EMPGs) with metallicities below $5\%\,Z_{\odot}$, representing a significant leap toward detecting the first galaxies without metals. However, accurate metallicity measurements require careful determination of physical conditions in the ionized gas. In this paper, we study four galaxies that appear to be EMPGs when analyzed using the direct $T_e$ method with the common low-density assumption ($n_e=10^3\,{\rm cm}^{-3}$). To test whether their metal-poor status holds when accurately measuring the density, we apply the direct method with a self-consistent determination of electron temperature ($T_e$) and density ($n_e$) in the high-ionization zone using the [OIII]$λ$5008, [OIII]$λ$4364, and [OIII]$λ$1666 lines, using JWST/NIRSpec data from the SPURS program in the Abell 2744 lensed field. We find that three out of four galaxies in our sample have extremely high electron densities ($n_e \sim 10^{5}-10^{6}\,{\rm cm^{-3}}$), which suppress the [OIII]$λ$5008 line and lead to underestimates of metallicity by up to $\sim1.1\,$dex when this density is not accounted for, and have true metallicities of 12+log(O/H) $\sim7.3-8.2$. Failure to account for high densities can therefore lead to systematic misclassification of metal-poor galaxies and biased conclusions about early chemical enrichment.

AI.tldr: Using JWST/NIRSpec data from the SPURS program, the authors analyze four candidate extremely metal-poor galaxies (EMPGs) in the Abell 2744 field. They find that three of the four have extremely high electron densities (n_e ~ 10^5-10^6 cm^-3), which suppress the [OIII]λ5008 line and cause metallicity underestimates of up to ~1.1 dex when density is not properly accounted for. Their true metallicities are 12+log(O/H) ~7.3-8.2, revealing that high densities can cause systematic misclassification of EMPGs.
AI.motivation: JWST has discovered dozens of extremely metal-poor galaxies, which are key targets for understanding the first metal-free galaxies. However, accurate metallicity determination requires proper treatment of physical conditions in the ionized gas. The authors aim to test whether the EMPG status of candidate galaxies holds when electron density is self-consistently measured rather than assumed at the common low-density value.
AI.method: The authors apply the direct T_e method with a self-consistent determination of both electron temperature and electron density in the high-ionization zone. This is done using the [OIII]λ5008, [OIII]λ4364, and [OIII]λ1666 lines from JWST/NIRSpec observations of four EMPG candidates from the SPURS program in the Abell 2744 lensed field, comparing results against the standard approach that assumes a fixed low density of n_e=10^3 cm^-3.
AI.result: Three out of four galaxies in the sample exhibit extremely high electron densities (n_e ~ 10^5-10^6 cm^-3). This high density suppresses the [OIII]λ5008 line and leads to metallicity underestimates of up to ~1.1 dex if density is not accounted for. The true metallicities are 12+log(O/H) ~7.3-8.2, meaning these galaxies are not as metal-poor as initially classified.
AI.conclusion: Failure to account for high electron densities can lead to systematic misclassification of metal-poor galaxies and biased conclusions about early chemical enrichment. Accurate density determination is essential for reliable metallicity measurements in high-redshift galaxies.

title: Early Planet Formation in Embedded Disks (eDisk). XXIV: Systematic Investigation of Disk Structures based on Visibility Analysis
comment: Accept to AJ. 47 pages, 10 Figures, 8 Tables
summary: The dust continuum emission from young protostellar disks encodes key information about their mass distribution and early evolution, yet uniform high-resolution comparative studies remain limited. We present a systematic uv-plane analysis of parametric intensity models applied to ALMA Band-6 (1.3 mm) observations of 23 disks (19 protostellar systems with 4 being in binary) from the eDisk sample, spanning Gaussian profiles to power-law cores with exponential tails (PLCT), including asymmetric extensions. Gaussian models generally fail to reproduce the centrally peaked emission and extended outer structure observed in most disks, whereas the PLCT framework provides a significantly improved description of radial brightness profiles. Incorporating azimuthal asymmetries further reduces residuals in 15 of 17 inclined disks, indicating that departures from axisymmetry are common at early stages. Only two disks, L1489 IRS and Oph IRS63, exhibit clear gap and ring substructures, while most appear smooth at the spatial resolution and sensitivity of our observations. These systems are among the most evolved in the sample, and the absence of flat-spectrum sources limits the evolutionary range probed, {suggesting that the detection of prominent gaps and rings is not common} in the earliest phases of disk evolution. Using a uniform definition of disk radius based on the 95\% enclosed flux, we find a positive correlation with stellar mass, $R_{\rm disk} \propto M_{\star}^{1.5 \pm 0.1}$, with disks in binary systems systematically smaller than those around isolated protostars. While the models capture overall morphology and large-scale asymmetries, distinguishing intrinsic structures from radiative transfer effects in optically thick regions remains challenging.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic uv-plane analysis of ALMA Band-6 (1.3 mm) observations of 23 protostellar disks from the eDisk sample using parametric intensity models (from Gaussians to PLCT profiles with azimuthal asymmetries). The PLCT framework significantly outperforms Gaussian models in reproducing radial brightness profiles. Only 2 of 23 disks (L1489 IRS and Oph IRS63) show clear gap/ring substructures, suggesting prominent substructures are not common in early disk evolution. The authors find a positive correlation of disk radius with stellar mass (R ∝ M*^1.5), with binary disks systematically smaller than isolated ones.
AI.motivation: Young protostellar disks' dust continuum emission encodes key information about their mass distribution and early evolution, yet uniform high-resolution comparative studies have remained limited. This work addresses the need for systematic, uniform analysis of early-stage disks to understand their structural properties and evolution.
AI.method: The authors performed systematic uv-plane analysis of parametric intensity models applied to ALMA Band-6 (1.3 mm) observations of 23 disks (19 protostellar systems, 4 binary) from the eDisk sample. Models ranged from simple Gaussians to power-law cores with exponential tails (PLCT), including azimuthal asymmetry extensions. Disk radii were defined using 95% enclosed flux.
AI.result: Gaussian models generally fail for most disks; PLCT models significantly improve radial brightness profile descriptions. Azimuthal asymmetries reduce residuals in 15 of 17 inclined disks. Only two disks (L1489 IRS and Oph IRS63) exhibit clear gap/ring substructures and are among the most evolved in the sample. A positive correlation R_disk ∝ M*^1.5±0.1 was found, with binary disks systematically smaller than isolated ones.
AI.conclusion: Prominent gap and ring substructures are not common in the earliest phases of disk evolution, but departures from axisymmetry are common early on. The sample's lack of flat-spectrum sources limits the evolutionary range probed. Distinguishing intrinsic structures from radiative transfer effects in optically thick regions remains challenging.
